1.1. Path A: Automated NCBI Datasets API
When configured with database: ncbi, the pipeline utilizes the official NCBI Datasets CLI tool (Sayers et al. 2022) to programmatically fetch data.

Sequence Download: The pipeline downloads the genomic datasets as a compressed zip package:
datasets download virus genome taxon "Influenza A virus" \
    --geo-location "Asia/Indonesia" \
    --include genome \
    --filename results/influenza-a-mp-universal/m01/ncbi_dataset.zip
Unzipping & Data Extraction: The genome sequences are extracted, and the structural data report is converted into tabular format using dataformat:
dataformat tsv virus-genome \
    --inputfile ncbi_dataset/data/data_report.jsonl \
    --fields accession,virus-name,geo-location,geo-region,collection-date,release-date,length,host-name \
    > results/influenza-a-mp-universal/m01/raw_metadata.jsonl
Column Mapping: The extracted tabular fields are mapped to Nextstrain Augur compatible naming conventions:

Accession \(\rightarrow\) strain
Virus Name \(\rightarrow\) virus
Geographic Location \(\rightarrow\) location
Geographic Region \(\rightarrow\) region
Collection Date \(\rightarrow\) date
Release Date \(\rightarrow\) date_submitted
Length \(\rightarrow\) length
Host Name \(\rightarrow\) host




1.2. Path B: Local / Manual Files (GISAID EpiFlu & Manual Portals)
When configured with database: local, the pipeline processes manually downloaded files, such as metadata sheets from GISAID (Shu and McCauley 2017).

Sequence Copy: Copies the raw FASTA file from the path specified in config["local_input"]["sequences"] to the pipeline directory.
Format-Aware Metadata Conversion:

NCBI Virus Web CSV: If format is ncbi_virus_csv, it maps columns and splits the combined Geo_Location (e.g., Indonesia: Java: Jakarta) into country (Indonesia) and region (Java).
TSV / GISAID: If format is gisaid_epiflu or gisaid_tsv, columns are copied as-is and forwarded to the downstream sanitizer.

title: Module 01: Data Acquisition
text:
2. Metadata Sanitization & 3-Tier Column Validation
Different databases output metadata with varying schemas, date formats, and missing entries. The Snakemake rule sanitize_metadata runs scripts/sanitize_metadata.py to normalize the tabular data into a consistent internal format using a 3-tier validation protocol:

Tier 1: Critical (strain, date, country)

Action: Must be present and valid. Any rows with empty strain IDs or completely unparseable dates (e.g., missing year) are dropped from the analysis to prevent pipeline failure.
Incomplete Dates: Imprecise dates like 2024 or 2024-05 are normalized to 2024-XX-XX or 2024-05-XX to comply with Nextstrain’s date format requirements.

Tier 2: Spatio-Temporal Context (region, host, division)

Action: Missing values are silently filled with defaults. If host is empty, it defaults to Human. If region is missing, it is derived from country mapping.

Tier 3: Metadata Pass-through

Action: Non-essential demographic fields (e.g., age, gender, passage_history) are passed through unmodified to maintain dataset richness.

title: Module 01: Data Acquisition
text:
3. Nextclade Clade & Lineage Classification
If Nextclade is enabled (nextclade.enabled: true in config), the raw sequences are aligned and classified using the Nextclade CLI tool (Aksamentov et al. 2021):

Dataset Retrieval: Fetches the specified Nextclade reference database (e.g., nextstrain/flu/h1n1pdm/ha/MW626062 for Influenza H1N1 HA):
nextclade dataset get --name "nextstrain/flu/h1n1pdm/ha/MW626062" --output-zip nextclade_dataset.zip
Nextclade Alignment & QC Run: Runs sequence alignment, mutation calling, clade classification, and frameshift detection:
nextclade run \
    --input-dataset nextclade_dataset.zip \
    --output-tsv nextclade.tsv \
    early_filtered_sequences.fasta
Metadata Enrichment: The rule enrich_metadata merges the base metadata table with the Nextclade output table (nextclade.tsv) using accession IDs, appending critical columns such as clade, subclade, and quality control scores (qc.overallStatus).

text:
5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. NCBI API Rate Limiting (HTTP 429)

Problem: Running the NCBI API pathway frequently fails with HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests.
Cause: NCBI limits unauthenticated requests to 3 per second.
Solution: Obtain an NCBI API Key from your NCBI account page and export it to your shell environment prior to executing the pipeline:
export NCBI_API_KEY="your_api_key_here"
This raises the rate limit to 10 requests per second.



5.2. Missing Package Dependencies in Nextclade

Problem: Nextclade CLI command is not found or fails to execute.
Solution: Ensure the Snakemake rule is running in the correct Conda environment (envs/nextstrain.yaml). If executing manually, nextclade can be installed via:
conda install -c conda-forge nextclade

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
Before biological wet-lab validation, designed primer and probe candidates must undergo virtual simulation to measure their diagnostic sensitivity. Module 10 executes the In-silico Validation Engine (scripts/m10_insilico_pcr.py) using SeqKit (Shen et al. 2016) to run high-throughput binding simulations against large GISAID and NCBI sequence databases.
This step calculates exact diagnostic coverage metrics broken down by subtype, collection year, and country to verify assay robustness against global and local viral diversity.

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
1. Virtual Amplification and Binding Simulation
The validation engine runs simulated amplifications by matching designed primers and probes against target database sequences using sequence-matching parameters:
                            ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                            │    final_candidates.json (M09)  │
                            └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │  In-silico Validation Engine │
                               │  (SeqKit Amplicon Simulator) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │  Target Database Sequences   │
                               │  (50k+ GISAID Fasta Genomes) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │   Mismatch Tolerance Filter  │
                               │  (3' Zone vs. Internal Body) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
                    ▼                                                 ▼
      ┌──────────────────────────┐                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
      │   Amplified Sequences    │                      │   Missed/Failed Strains  │
      │   (Simulated Positive)   │                      │   (Diagnostic Escape)    │
      └──────────────────────────┘                      └──────────────────────────┘

1.1. PCR Simulation (seqkit amplicon)
SeqKit’s amplicon command matches primer sequences against every target genome in the database, allowing up to a defined number of mismatches (default: \(3\) or \(4\) mismatches). It returns virtual amplicons for target genomes that match both primers within a designated length range (e.g. 100–300 bp).


1.2. RAA Isothermal Binding Rules
Because RAA operates at \(39^\circ\text{C}\) with a recombinase complex, it is thermodynamically tolerant of minor internal mismatches but highly sensitive to 3’ terminal defects. The engine implements strict, multi-zone mismatch criteria:

3’ Critical Zone: Evaluates the last 4 nucleotides of the 3’ end (the recombinase “anchor region”) of both primers, allowing a maximum of 1 mismatch; more than 1 vetoes binding. The 4-nt window follows Higgins et al. (2022) — the only study to characterise primer–template mismatches specifically for RPA — which found single mismatches outside the terminal anchor do not significantly affect time-to-positivity. The earlier 8-nt value had no source and under-reported coverage.
Internal Body: Allows a maximum of 4 mismatches across the rest of the 30–35 bp primer body.
Probe Binding: Probes (46–52 bp) allow a maximum of 5 total mismatches (not 3’-weighted — the probe’s 3’ terminus is C3-blocked and cannot be extended), following the TwistAmp Assay Design Manual §2.7, which reports RPA performance is unaffected by 5–9 mismatches on primers or probe.



1.3. RAA is decoupled from the PCR gate; the H5N1 gap is a real clade mismatch
An earlier version of M10 took its amplification call only from seqkit amplicon run at the PCR budget (max_mismatch = 3) and then applied the RAA rules only to sequences seqkit had already amplified — so raa_detected_pct was a subset of PCR and could never exceed it, the opposite of RAA biology. That has been fixed: M10 now runs seqkit at the wider RAA mismatch budget and derives the PCR and RAA metrics separately, so RAA can exceed PCR where the chemistry allows. In the current indo-only run RAA (93.14%) now sits above PCR (91.47%) overall, and RAA raises the divergent-but-close subtypes (e.g. A/H9N2 91→99%).
What the decoupling did not change is global A/H5N1, which stays at ~32% on both PCR (31.84%) and RAA (31.89%). This is therefore not a modelling artifact — it is a genuine clade mismatch. indo-only covers local A/H5N1 at 98.72% (the focal DB, §3), so the primers work on the H5N1 they were built on; but Indonesian H5N1 is clade 2.1.3 (older poultry outbreaks) while global H5N1 is now dominated by clade 2.3.4.4b (the 2021+ panzootic), which differs beyond even the RAA mismatch tolerance. The per-position attribution (M12, scripts/m12_coverage_attribution.py, under results/<build>/m12/ and in the QC dossier) localises the failing global H5N1 to clade 2.3.4.4b. Closing it would require adding recent clade-2.3.4.4b sequences to the design cohort — a targeted update, not a routine-use fix.

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
2. Spatial and Temporal Coverage Aggregation
To identify potential diagnostic gaps, the engine aggregates simulation results into distinct metadata dimensions:

Subtype Coverage: Breaks down detection percentages by viral sub-lineages (e.g., A/H1N1, A/H3N2, A/H5N1) to ensure the assay is truly universal.
Temporal Coverage: Groups detection rates by year of sequence collection (e.g., 2015 to 2025) to track whether modern evolutionary mutations are lowering assay sensitivity over time.
Spatial Coverage: Groups detection rates by country (e.g., Indonesia vs. global) to guarantee high local diagnostic sensitivity.

5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. RAA coverage reads at or below PCR for a subtype

Problem: A subtype’s RAA amplified percentage does not exceed its PCR percentage.
Was an artifact, now fixed: earlier M10 evaluated RAA only on sequences the PCR seqkit -m max_mismatch pass had already amplified, so RAA was a subset of PCR and could never exceed it. M10 now runs seqkit at the RAA budget and derives PCR and RAA separately (see §1.3), so RAA exceeds PCR wherever the extra mismatch tolerance helps (e.g. indo-only overall RAA 93.14% > PCR 91.47%).
If RAA still ≈ PCR for a subtype, it is real: the divergence exceeds even the RAA tolerance. The clearest case is global A/H5N1 (~32% on both) — a clade mismatch (local clade 2.1.3 vs global clade 2.3.4.4b), not a modelling limit. Use the Module 12 attribution to localise it, and a targeted design update (adding the divergent clade) rather than expecting the model to close the gap.

3. How to Interpret & Validate Reference Alignments
The reference genome acts as the “anchor” for the entire pipeline. During Module 03 (Alignment), the raw sequences are mapped against the reference:

Coordinate Drift: If the selected reference sequence is too divergent from the target population (e.g. using a 1934 H1N1 reference for a 2026 seasonal design), the alignment will suffer from excessive gaps. This will cause coordinate mismatch downstream.
CDS Mapping: Ensure the references.annotation matches the reference sequence exactly. If the coordinates in the GFF file do not match the exons in the FASTA reference, the translation step in Module 05 (Selection Pressure) will fail, producing frame-shift errors or early stop codons in the HyPhy input.







ImportantVerification Step



Before initiating a run, verify that the reference FASTA header matches the GFF sequence ID exactly (e.g. both must read NC_002016.1). If they do not match, Snakemake will crash in Module 03 due to reference header mismatch.

title: Scientific Literature
text: This section provides the scientific rationale, mathematical formulations, and literature background supporting the methodology used in our target discovery pipeline.

title: Scientific Literature
section: 1. Molecular Diagnostics: Beyond Static Shannon Entropy
text:
1. Molecular Diagnostics: Beyond Static Shannon Entropy
Traditional molecular diagnostic design relies almost exclusively on sequence conservation metrics calculated from contemporary isolates, most notably Shannon Entropy (Equation 1).
\[H(x) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i) \log_2 P(x_i)\]
Where \(P(x_i)\) is the probability of observing nucleotide or amino acid \(x_i\) at alignment position \(x\).

The Limitations of Shannon Entropy
While Shannon Entropy is effective at measuring static sequence conservation, it suffers from critical limitations:

Temporal Blindness: Entropy only captures variation at a single snapshot in time. It cannot distinguish between a position that is temporarily conserved due to sampling bias or recent clonal expansion, and one that is conserved due to strict functional constraints.
Lack of Functional Context: It treats all mutations equally, failing to capture the biological fitness costs associated with specific nucleotide substitutions (Capra and Singh 2007). For instance, a conservative mutation (maintaining residue properties) is weighted identically to a disruptive one.



Diagnostic Escape and Primer Mismatches
In clinical diagnostics, relying on static conservation frequently leads to diagnostic escape or signature erosion. Studies on SARS-CoV-2 PCR assays demonstrated that circulating genomic mutations rapidly accumulate at primer and probe binding sites, significantly reducing binding affinity and leading to false-negative clinical results (Khan and Cheung 2020).
Crucially, mutations located at the 3’ terminus of the primers have the most detrimental effect on PCR amplification, as they directly impede the extension activity of DNA polymerases (Vanaerschot et al. 2020). This makes structural and selection-aware design a vital tool to future-proof diagnostic targets.


The Evolutionary-Aware Paradigm
To overcome these limitations, our pipeline integrates evolutionary dynamics:

Purifying Selection Detection: By mapping codon-by-codon evolutionary selection pressures, we identify target sites under strict purifying selection (\(dN/dS \ll 1\)). Mutations at these sites are functionally deleterious to the pathogen, meaning any mutant strain is rapidly eliminated by natural selection.
Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction (ASR): By reconstructing the historical ancestral states at internal nodes of the phylogenetic tree, we trace the evolutionary inertia of genomic regions. Target regions with high ancestral-to-contemporary conservation (high Bridge Score) represent genomic zones that have remained locked across evolutionary time, making them highly resilient to future mutations.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
2. Research Design & Workflow Framework
Designing a pipeline capable of processing thousands of viral genomes with strict reproducibility requires a robust framework. Below is the scientific justification for our software architecture choices:

2.1. Snakemake: Workflow Orchestration & Reproducibility
For enterprise-grade diagnostic target discovery, script-based pipelines are insufficient. We utilize Snakemake (Mölder et al. 2021) as our workflow management system.

Deterministic Dependency Resolution: Snakemake isolates each execution module (M01-M10) into distinct conda environments, preventing package version mismatch.
Traceability and Log Auditing: Every step records CLI inputs, environment parameters, and logs, ensuring the pipeline meets clinical validation standards.



2.2. Nextstrain: Spatio-Temporal Genomic Surveillance
For tracking pathogen lineages globally, we utilize the Nextstrain architecture (Hadfield et al. 2018).

Clade and Lineage Definition: Nextstrain provides real-time tracking of emerging variants, allowing us to select representative datasets.
Phylogeographic Subsampling: To avoid geographic bias, we subsample sequences relative to case numbers and demographic travel data (informed by BPS data), preventing overrepresented sequences from skewing conservation scores.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
3. Core Bioinformatics Algorithms

3.1. Alignment: MAFFT (Multiple Sequence Alignment)
Aligning thousands of viral genomes requires high speed without sacrificing alignment quality at the codon level.

Algorithm: We use MAFFT (Katoh and Standley 2013), applying the progressive method FFT-NS-2 for large datasets and iterative refinement (L-INS-i) for sub-datasets. MAFFT’s fast Fourier transform approximation allows rapid alignment of highly variable regions while preserving structural codon boundaries.



3.2. Phylogeny and ASR: IQ-TREE 2
Phylodynamic tree reconstruction and ancestral sequence states are computed using IQ-TREE 2 (Minh et al. 2020).

Substitution Model Selection: IQ-TREE 2 integrates ModelFinder to automatically select the optimal nucleotide or codon substitution model (e.g., GTR+I+G4) based on Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).
Ancestral Reconstruction: IQ-TREE 2 utilizes Empirical Bayes maximum likelihood methods to perform marginal and joint ancestral sequence reconstruction at all phylogenetic nodes, providing the raw inputs for our Bridge Scoring engine.



3.3. Selection Pressure: HyPhy (Hypothesis Testing using Phylogenies)
To calculate site-specific selection pressures, we use HyPhy (Pond et al. 2020).

FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian Approximation): FUBAR (Murrell et al. 2013) employs a fast Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to calculate the posterior probability of purifying selection (\(dN < dS\)) at each codon site. FUBAR is selected for its high processing speed on large alignments.
MEME (Mixed Effects Model of Episodic Selection): MEME (Murrell et al. 2012) is used to detect codons experiencing transient, episodic positive selection along a fraction of branches, ensuring we filter out target regions susceptible to localized adaptation.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
4. Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RAA/RPA) Design
Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) and its close derivative, Recombinase Amplification Assay (RAA), operate isothermally (typically at 37–42°C) (Piepenburg et al. 2006).

Diagnostic Oligonucleotide Requirements
RAA chemistry demands distinct target parameters compared to conventional PCR:

Primer Length: RAA primers are significantly longer (30–35 bp) than PCR primers (18–22 bp).
Probe Length: RAA probes (typically Exo probes) require a length of 46–52 bp with internal fluorophores and quencher modifications.
Thermodynamic Mismatch Tolerance: Because RAA operates isothermally, longer primers exhibit a substantial tolerance to template mismatches, successfully amplifying sequences even with multiple mismatches (up to 9 mismatches across primer/probe binding sites) (Daher et al. 2016). However, mismatches located at the 3’ terminus of RAA primers still significantly reduce amplification kinetics, requiring the target site to be located on extremely conserved regions to maintain maximum sensitivity. We calculate these parameters using nearest-neighbor thermodynamic models to exclude stable secondary structures.
